2 Samuel — Book introduction (Modern English production candidate)

This book records the reign of King David.

It describes his victories, Israel's increasing prosperity and his efforts to reform the nation's religious life.

It also records the serious sins David committed and the troubles that came upon his family and his nation as punishment.

Many events in this history deserve to be imitated, while others were written to warn us.

Scripture gives a truthful account of David's reign rather than concealing his failures.

Anyone who weighs his many virtues and excellent qualities fairly alongside his faults will recognize him as a great and godly man.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesTidings brought to David of the death of Saul.1–10The Amalekite is put to death.11–16David's lamentation for Saul and Jonathan.17–27
David receives news of Saul's death (verses 1–10)

The event that opened David's way to the throne happened at about the same time he was suffering severe distress.

People who have entrusted their concerns to the Lord can wait quietly for his will to be done.

David's response showed that he had not desired Saul's death and had not grown impatient to receive the kingdom.

The Amalekite is put to death (verses 11–16)

David genuinely mourned Saul.

All those with him humbled themselves beneath God's hand, which had fallen heavily upon Israel in its defeat.

David ordered the man who brought the news to be executed because the man had confessed to murdering the king.

Henry argues that David did not act unjustly in this case.

If the Amalekite's account was true, the man had committed treason and deserved death under the law of that time.

But if he had lied to David, the lie had brought about his own death.

So lies will sooner or later turn against the people who tell them.

David showed zeal for public justice without allowing his own personal advantage to influence the matter.

David laments Saul and Jonathan (verses 17–27)

Henry thinks Kasheth, meaning “the bow,” was probably the title of David's funeral song.

David did not praise Saul for virtues he had not possessed.

In particular, he said nothing about Saul's religious devotion or personal goodness.

Yet Jonathan had been a dutiful son and Saul an affectionate father, and they loved one another.

David had good reason to say that Jonathan's love for him had been extraordinary.

Next to the love shared between Christ and his people, the affection that flows from such love produces the strongest friendships.

The suffering of God's people and the victories of his enemies always grieve true believers, even when those events may bring the believers personal advantage.
classic_reading:
[2Sam.1.1-2Sam.1.10]
2 Samuel
This book is the history of the reign of king David. It relates his victories, the growth of the prosperity of Israel, and his reformation of the state of religion. With these events are recorded the grievous sins he committed, and the family as well as public troubles with which he was punished. We here meet with many things worthy of imitation, and many that are written for our warning. The history of king David is given in Scripture with much faithfulness, and from it he appears, to those who fairly balance his many virtues and excellent qualities against his faults, to have been a great and good man.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
Tidings brought to David of the death of Saul. | (1-10) |
The Amalekite is put to death. | (11-16) |
David's lamentation for Saul and Jonathan. | (17-27) |
Verses 1-10
The blow which opened David's way to the throne was given about the time he had been sorely distressed. Those who commit their concerns to the Lord, will quietly abide his will. It shows that he desired not Saul's death, and he was not impatient to come to the throne.
[2Sam.1.11-2Sam.1.16]
Verses 11-16
David was sincere in his mourning for Saul; and all with him humbled themselves under the hand of God, laid so heavily upon Israel by this defeat. The man who brought the tidings, David put to death, as a murderer of his prince. David herein did not do unjustly; the Amalekite confessed the crime. If he did as he said, he deserved to die for treason; and his lying to David, if indeed it were a lie, proved, as sooner or later that sin will prove, lying against himself. Hereby David showed himself zealous for public justice, without regard to his own private interest.
[2Sam.1.17-2Sam.1.27]
Verses 17-27
Kasheth, or "the bow," probably was the title of this mournful, funeral song. David does not commend Saul for what he was not; and says nothing of his piety or goodness. Jonathan was a dutiful son, Saul an affectionate father, therefore dear to each other. David had reason to say, that Jonathan's love to him was wonderful. Next to the love between Christ and his people, that affection which springs form it, produces the strongest friendship. The trouble of the Lord's people, and triumphs of his enemies, will always grieve true believers, whatever advantages they may obtain by them.

David is made king at Hebron (verses 1–7)

After Saul died, many people gathered around David at Ziklag (1 Chronicles 12:22).

But David trusted the Lord, who had promised him the kingdom, to give it in the proper time and way.

Confidence in God's promise does not discourage diligent effort.

It encourages it.

Someone chosen for the crown of life should not say, “Then I need do nothing.”

Rather, that person should say, “Then I will do everything God directs me to do.”

David made this use of his calling, and all whom God chooses should do likewise.

When we travel or move to a new home, it is a great comfort to know the Lord goes before us.

We may have that confidence when faith and prayer set him before us.

God directed David's steps as promised.

David's rise was gradual.

In the same way, the kingdom of the Messiah, the Son of David, advances by stages.

Christ already is Lord of all, though we do not yet see everything subjected to him.

Abner supports Ish-bosheth; civil war begins (verses 8–17)

Most of Israel refused to recognize David.

The Lord used that rejection to train his servant for later responsibility and usefulness.

David's conduct under repeated difficulties displayed the strength of genuine godliness.

He was a picture of Christ, whom Israel would not receive even though the Father had anointed him as Prince and Savior.

Abner suggested that the young soldiers should “play” before the leaders.

But he was proposing a deadly contest.

Fools make a game out of sin.

Anyone who treats human bloodshed as entertainment is unworthy of being called human.

Asahel pursues Abner and dies (verses 18–24)

Death often approaches by a path we do not expect.

The very abilities we take the greatest pride in can become our undoing.

Asahel's speed, which he trusted so confidently, did not save him.

Instead, it hastened his death.

The rival armies withdraw (verses 25–32)

Abner appealed to Joab to consider the terrible consequences of civil war.

Those who make light of such unnatural conflict will eventually find it bitter for everyone involved.

People easily appeal to reason when it benefits them, though they refused to listen to reason when it worked against their interests.

Notice how quickly a change in circumstances can change a person's opinion.

What seemed enjoyable in the morning can appear dreadful by night.

Those most eager to enter a dispute often regret it before it ends.

They would have done better to avoid the quarrel at the start, as Solomon counsels.

The same is true of every sin.

Would that people considered early enough how bitter its outcome will be!

The account mentions Asahel's burial.

People distinguish the graves and remains of important individuals from those of others.

But at the resurrection only one distinction will endure forever: godly or ungodly.

Abner appeals to Joab concerning the miserable consequences of a civil war. Those who make light of such unnatural contests, will find that they are bitterness to all concerned. The same thing which looked pleasant in the morning, at night looked dismal. David grows stronger (verses 1–6)

The long conflict tested David's faith and patience.

When he finally established his kingdom, the blessing was all the more welcome because he had waited for it.

This struggle pictures the war between grace and corruption in the hearts of believers.

It is a long conflict.

The flesh desires what opposes the Spirit, and the Spirit opposes the flesh.

As God's work of holiness progresses, corruption gradually grows weaker—like the household of Saul—while grace grows stronger, like the household of David.

Abner leaves Ish-bosheth for David (verses 7–21)

Many people commit disgraceful offenses but are too proud to bear correction or even the suspicion that they may be guilty.

Those who continue in sin while pretending not to care often know within themselves that they are fighting against God.

Some pursue only their own advantage.

They will betray the people who trust them when they see something to gain.

Even through people driven by revenge, ambition or sinful desire, the Lord can carry out his own purposes.

But because such people do not intend to honor him, they may ultimately be cast aside with contempt.

David's willingness to receive Michal showed generosity both toward her and toward the memory of Saul.

He probably recalled that he had once owed his life to her love.

He also knew her separation from him had occurred partly through her father's authority.

No one should set his heart upon someone or something to which he has no rightful claim.

If disagreement has separated husband and wife, those who desire God's blessing should seek reconciliation and live together in love.

Joab murders Abner; David mourns (verses 22–39)

Abner had acted scornfully, and judgment awaited him.

Yet Joab's killing of him was wicked.

David was deeply distressed by the murder and publicly demonstrated his hatred of the crime.

The guilt of murder can bring a curse upon families.

If human courts fail to hold murderers accountable, God will.

People act foolishly when they shorten their own days or make no preparation for the world to come.

How desirable is human authority, really?

A ruler can hold the title and bear responsibility, yet find his ability to do right severely limited.

David should have performed his duty and then trusted God with the outcome.

But worldly calculation led him to spare Joab.

The Son of David may delay judgment for a long time.

He will never fail to judge unrepentant sinners.

The One who now reigns on David's throne possesses a much greater kingdom.

Everything he does is observed with joy by those who willingly belong to him.

Judgments are prepared for such scorners as Abner; but Joab, in what he did, acted wickedly. David laid Abner's murder deeply to heart, and in many ways expressed his detestation of it. The guilt of blood brings a curse upon families: if men do not avenge it, God will. It is a sad thing to die like a fool, as they do that any way shorten their own days, and those who make no provision for another world. Ish-bosheth is murdered (verses 1–7)

Consider how Ish-bosheth was killed!

When difficulties arise, they should encourage us to act wisely and vigorously.

If instead they drain away our courage and effort, we may lose both our earthly lives and the heavenly crowns toward which we should be striving.

Do not love sleep so much that it leads to poverty and ruin.

A soul made idle is an easy target for the destroyer.

None of us knows where or when death will come.

Whenever we lie down to sleep, we cannot be certain we will wake again.

Nor can we know from whose hand death may reach us.

David judges the murderers (verses 8–12)

We may be glad to receive something to which we have a rightful claim while sincerely grieving over the unlawful means by which it came into our hands.

We may mourn the death of a person even if that death appears to benefit us.

The men who killed Ish-bosheth shed innocent blood for wicked, self-interested reasons.

David was right, in Henry's judgment, to carry out the historical punishment against them.

He refused to accept help toward the throne when it came through wrongdoing.

The Lord had already brought David through many difficulties and dangers.

David trusted him to complete the work he had begun, without the help of criminal schemes.

David spoke of being delivered from every adversity as though it were already accomplished.

He knew that the God who had delivered him in the past would continue to deliver him, though many storms still lay ahead.

David becomes king over all Israel (verses 1–5)

David was now anointed king for the third time.

His rise had been gradual so that his faith could be tested and he could gain experience.

In this way his rule pictured the kingdom of the Messiah, which also grows toward its full glory by stages.

Jesus became our Brother.

He took our human nature and lived within it so that he could become our Prince and Savior.

A humbled sinner can take courage from this close and loving relationship.

Such a person seeks his salvation, submits to his authority and asks for his protection.

David takes Zion (verses 6–10)

God's enemies often feel most confident in their strength shortly before their fall.

The pride and insults of the Jebusites stirred David to action, and the Lord God of hosts was with him.

Similarly, on the day of God's power, Satan's stronghold—the human heart—can become God's dwelling through the Spirit.

It becomes the throne on which the Son of David rules and brings every thought into obedience to himself.

May Christ enter our hearts, claim them, cleanse them, overthrow every idol and reign forever!

God establishes David's kingdom (verses 11–16)

David's house was not made less holy or less fit to be dedicated to God because foreign builders helped construct it.

The gospel church is described in similar language:

The sons of foreigners will rebuild its walls, and their kings will serve it (Isaiah 60:10).

David's kingdom became firmly established.

Likewise, the Son of David reigns securely, as do those who through him are made kings and priests to God.

Israel had never appeared so great as it did at this time.

Many people enjoy God's favor and love without recognizing it and therefore miss the comfort they might have had.

To receive his favor and know that we have it is great happiness.

David recognized that God had raised him to power for the good of his people, so he could bless them and they could live happily under his leadership.

David defeats the Philistines (verses 17–25)

The Philistines overlooked the fact that David enjoyed God's presence, which Saul had lost.

In the same way, as soon as the Messiah's kingdom was established in the world, it came under attack from powers of darkness.

Nations raged and rulers stood against it, but in vain (Psalm 2:1).

The eventual defeat would fall upon Satan's own kingdom.

David confessed his dependence upon God for victory.

He asked whether the Lord would fight for him and submitted to God's decision.

The promise of victory over our spiritual enemies should give us courage in spiritual conflict.

David waited until God moved.

Then he acted—but not before.

He was being trained in dependence on God and his providence.

The Lord performed what he had promised, and David made good use of every opportunity provided.

Likewise, before the apostles began their work against Satan's kingdom, they had to wait for the promised Spirit.

He came upon them with a sound from heaven like a rushing, powerful wind (Acts 2:2).

David was anointed king a third time. His advances were gradual, that his faith might be tried, and that he might gain experience. Thus his kingdom typified that of the Messiah, which was to come to its height by degrees. Thus Jesus became our Brother, took upon him our nature, dwelt in it that he might become our Prince and Saviour: thus the humbled sinner takes encouragement from the endearing relation, applies for his salvation, submits to his authority, and craves his protection.

Verses 6-10
The enemies of God's people are often very confident of their own strength, and most secure when their day to fall draws nigh. But the pride and insolence of the Jebusites animated David, and the Lord God of hosts was with him. Thus in the day of God's power, Satan's strong-hold, the human heart, is changed into a habitation of God through the Spirit, and into a throne on which the Son of David rules, and brings every thought into obedience to himself. May He thus come, and claim, and cleanse, each of our hearts; and, destroying every idol, may he reign there for ever!
[2Sam.5.11-2Sam.5.16]
Verses 11-16
David's house was not the worse, nor the less fit to be dedicated to God, for being built by the sons of the stranger. It is prophesied of the gospel church, The sons of strangers shall build up thy walls, and their kings shall minister unto thee, [Isa.60.10] Is 60:10. David's government was rooted and built up. David was established king; so is the Son of David, and all who, through him, are made to our God kings and priests. Never had the nation of Israel appeared so great as it began now to be. Many have the favour and love of God, yet do not perceive it, and so want the comfort of it; but to be exalted to that, and to perceive it, is happiness. David owned it was for his people's sake God had done great things for him; that he might be a blessing to them, and that they might be happy under him.
[2Sam.5.17-2Sam.5.25]

The Philistines considered not that David had the presence of God with him, which Saul had forfeited and lost. The kingdom of the Messiah, as soon as it was set up in the world, was thus attacked by the powers of darkness. The heathen raged, and the kings of the earth set themselves to oppose it; but all in vain, [Ps.2.1] Psa 2:1, &c. The destruction will turn, as this did, upon Satan's own kingdom. David owns dependence on God for victory; and refers himself to the good pleasure of God, Wilt thou do it? The assurance God has given us of victory over our spiritual enemies, should encourage us in our spiritual conflicts. David waited till God moved; he stirred then, but not till then. He was trained up in dependence on God and his providence. God performed his promise, and David failed not to improve his advantages. When the kingdom of the Messiah was to be set up, the apostles, who were to beat down the devil's kingdom, must not attempt any thing till they received the promise of the Spirit; who came with a sound from heaven, as of a rushing, mighty wind, [Acts.2.2] Ac 2:2.

David's prayer breathes deep love and devotion toward God.

He thought humbly of his own merits.

Everything we possess must be regarded as a divine gift.

David spoke with great reverence and gratitude about the Lord's favor.

Considering what human beings are, and their fallen condition, it is astonishing that God should deal so graciously with them.

The promise of Christ contains every blessing.

God knows us better than we know ourselves.

Let us therefore be satisfied with his dealings.

David defeats surrounding nations (verses 1–8)

David subdued the Philistines, who had troubled Israel for many years.

In the same way, after the saints have fought long and often against the powers of darkness, the Son of David will place those enemies beneath their feet and make them more than conquerors.

David also defeated the Moabites and made them pay tribute.

Two portions were destroyed, and a third was spared.

Henry urges that the line of mercy should be stretched as far as possible.

David also defeated the Syrians.

The Lord preserved him through these wars, and in his psalms David repeatedly gave God the glory for his victories.

The captured treasures are dedicated to God (verses 9–14)

David set apart the precious things he obtained for the future construction of the temple.

He had destroyed the golden idols of the Philistines (2 Samuel 5:21), but dedicated the golden vessels to God's service.

The grace of the Son of David acts in a similar way when it wins a soul.

Everything that stands opposed to God must be destroyed.

Every sinful desire must be put to death and crucified.

But whatever can honor God should be dedicated to him.

In this way its purpose and rightful ownership are changed.

God employs his servants differently.

Some, like David, fight battles.

Others, like Solomon, build.

One servant prepares work that another completes, and God receives the glory for both.

David governs with justice (verses 15–18)

David neither committed injustice nor withheld or delayed justice from anyone.

He worked diligently and was ready to receive requests and appeals.

He judged without favoritism.

In these qualities he pictured Jesus Christ.

Let us submit to Christ, seek his friendship and regard his service as our joy.

Let us diligently perform the duties he has given each of us.

David appointed his sons to important positions of authority.

But believers, who are Christ's spiritual descendants, receive still greater honor.

Through him they are made kings and priests to God (Revelation 1:6).

David remembers Jonathan's family (verses 1–8)

Amid many responsibilities, we easily forget the gratitude we owe and the promises we have made—not only to our friends, but to God himself.

Yet people whose faith is genuine cannot remain content until they fulfill these duties.

The people who most deserve practical kindness and charity do not always come to our attention without some effort to find them.

Jonathan had been David's friend, bound by solemn promise.

David therefore sought out Jonathan's son Mephibosheth to show him kindness.

God remains faithful to us.

We must not act unfaithfully toward one another.

If Providence lifts us into a better position while our friends or their families suffer poverty or disgrace, we should regard this change as an especially good opportunity to help them.

David provides for Mephibosheth (verses 9–13)

David pictured Jesus Christ, who is both David's Lord and Son—his Root and Offspring.

David's kindness to Mephibosheth therefore reminds us of God's astonishing love toward fallen humanity.

David owed something to Jonathan because of their covenant.

God, however, was under no such obligation to save sinners.

The Son of God came looking for a lost and ruined human race.

Human beings were not seeking him.

He came to seek and to save them.
